explication:
<explanation>
1. Identify the project type and purpose  
   - This is an open-source integration tool (“BlenderMCP”) that connects Blender (a 3D modeling application) to Claude AI via the Model Context Protocol (MCP). It consists of a Blender addon and a standalone Python MCP server.  

2. Analyze the file structure  
   Top-level files and directories:
   • addon.py    – Blender addon script that runs inside Blender  
   • main.py    – entry point for the CLI tool (“blender-mcp”)  
   • assets/    – screenshots and UI instruction images  
   • src/blender_mcp/server.py – MCP server implementation  
   • pyproject.toml, uv.lock – build/runtime configuration  

   Patterns and configuration:
   • addon.py loads a socket server in Blender.  
   • server.py listens for MCP commands and forwards them over TCP.  
   • The CLI (uvx command) launches main.py → server.py.  

3. Extract architectural insights from README  
   – Two-way JSON-over-TCP protocol (“type”/“params” commands, “status”/“result” responses).  
   – External integrations:  
     • Claude AI (as an MCP client)  
     • Poly Haven assets API  
     • Hyper3D Rodin API  
   – User workflows: Blender UI → socket → MCP server → Claude and back.  

4. Main components and interactions for the diagram  
   a. Components  
      1. Blender Application  
         – BlenderMCP Addon (addon.py)  
         – UI in 3D View sidebar  
         – Local TCP socket listener (e.g., localhost:port)  
      2. MCP Server Process  
         – CLI entry (uvx → main.py)  
         – server.py implements protocol, manages sockets  
      3. Claude AI Desktop/Cursor  
         – Configured as an MCP client pointing to “blender-mcp”  
      4. External Services  
         – Poly Haven API  
         – Hyper3D Rodin API  
   b. Relationships and data flow  
      1. User clicks “Connect” in Blender → addon.py starts the socket server  
      2. MCP Server (CLI) registers with Claude → Claude sends JSON commands  
      3. server.py forwards commands over TCP to Blender addon  
      4. Blender executes commands (object creation, material changes, code exec)  
      5. Results/responses are sent back over the same TCP channel → MCP server → Claude  
      6. For asset/model requests, MCP server or addon calls out to Poly Haven / Hyper3D endpoints  
   c. Architectural patterns / design principles  
      – Separation of concerns: Blender-embedded addon vs. external protocol server  
      – Simple JSON-over-TCP protocol for interoperability  
      – CLI wrapper (uvx) for process management  
      – Extensibility via external service adapters (APIs)  
   d. Key technologies  
      – Python 3.10+  
      – TCP sockets, JSON serialization  
      – Blender Python API (bpy)  
      – uv (Astral UV package manager to publish “blender-mcp” CLI)  

5. Diagram guidelines tailored to this integration tool  
   • Emphasize core layers:  
     – UI & addon layer (inside Blender)  
     – Protocol/server layer (outside Blender)  
     – AI client layer (Claude Desktop or Cursor)  
     – External asset/model APIs  
   • Show the TCP socket as the communication backbone between addon and server  
   • Highlight extension points: Poly Haven and Hyper3D integrations  

6. Visual diagram best practices  
   – Use clear, distinct shapes:  
     • Rounded rectangle for Blender application  
     • Cylinder for external APIs (Poly Haven, Hyper3D)  
     • Rectangle with gear icon for MCP Server  
     • Cloud icon for Claude AI  
   – Label each component with name and tech (e.g., “BlenderMCP Addon (addon.py, bpy)”)  
   – Draw directional arrows for data flow:  
     1. Claude → MCP Server → Blender  
     2. Blender → MCP Server → Claude  
     3. MCP Server ↔ External APIs  
   – Color-code layers:  
     • UI/Add-on (blue)  
     • Protocol/Server (green)  
     • AI client (orange)  
     • External services (purple)  

7. Detailed breakdown for the principal engineer  
   1. Start by sketching a vertical swimlane or horizontal tier diagram.  
   2. Place “Blender + addon.py” in one tier; show internal socket listener.  
   3. In the next tier, draw “blender-mcp” server (main.py → server.py) labeled with uvx.  
   4. At the top, draw “Claude AI” as a client consuming the MCP server.  
   5. Off to the side, place “Poly Haven API” and “Hyper3D Rodin API” with arrows into the server or addon depending on who invokes them.  
   6. Annotate arrow labels: “JSON Command(type, params)”, “JSON Response(status, result)”, “HTTP REST calls for assets/models.”  
   7. Use a legend to define shapes and colors.  

By following these guidelines, you’ll produce an accurate, detailed architecture diagram that highlights every critical component, their interactions, and the underlying protocols and external dependencies of the BlenderMCP project.  
</explanation>
